{{Short description|Lithuanian philosopher (1776–1835)}}
'''Anioł Dowgird''' ({{langx|lt|Angelas Daugirdas|link=no}}; 1776–1835) was a [[philosopher]] of [[Enlightenment in Poland|Polish Enlightenment]] and Lithuanian Enlightenment.

Born into a noble family in the Mahiliou province, Dowgird studied in [[Jesuit]] and [[Piarist]] schools in [[Mscislau]], [[Mahiliou]] and [[Dubrowna|Dubrouna]], then joined the [[Piarist Order]] and took [[holy orders]]. Subsequently, he taught at Piarist schools and for a time was a professor of [[logic]] and [[ethics]] at [[Vilnius University]].<ref name=wiep>"Dowgird, Anioł," ''Wielka Ilustrowana Encyklopedia Powszechna'' (Great Illustrated Universal Encyclopedia), volume IV.</ref>

Dowgird derived his views from [[John Locke]]'s [[empiricism]], the [[Scottish School of Common Sense]],<ref>"Dowgird, Anioł," ''Encyklopedia Powszechna PWN'' (PWN Universal Encyclopedia), vol. 1, p. 615.</ref> and [[Immanuel Kant]]'s ''[[Critique of Pure Reason]]''. But, unlike Kant, he ascribed to time and space a real existence independent of man.<ref name=wiep />

==Works==
*''O logice, metafizyce i filozofji moralnej'' (On Logic, Metaphysics and Moral Philosophy)
*''Wykład przyrodzonych myślenia prawideł, czyli logika teoretyczna i praktyczna'' (A Treatise on the Natural Laws of Thought, or Theoretical and Practical Logic)
*''Rezczywistość poznań ludzkich'' (The Reality of Human Experience)<ref name=wiep />

He also wrote several sermons and left a manuscript treatise on [[Immanuel Kant|Kant]]'s philosophy.<ref name=wiep />
